hero.highlight.text: ask a question only old information can answer.

hero.takeaway.text: There are three common ways to rewrite old history shorter, and each loses information differently. Use a question that only the earliest tool result can answer to check whether that information is still there.

concepts.01-rule.description.text: The program assembles the goal, constraints, source, fact, and to-dos into one record by fixed fields; if the key evidence does not fit, it raises an error.

concepts.02-clear.description.text: Earlier tool results stay in place with their content replaced by a "cleared" note; the call and the tool result are still paired.

concepts.03-summary.description.text: Send one extra request that has the model write the earlier conversation as a summary; what stays is up to the model.

concepts.04-probe.description.text: A question only the earliest tool result can answer. Ask it again after compression to learn whether that information is still there.

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Old content that does not fit can be dropped as a whole group, or it can be rewritten shorter and kept. That is context compression. The truncation window in {{lesson:context-budget}} can only drop: it fills from the newest message backward, and the group that does not fit is thrown out entirely. With the default budget, the first thing dropped is exactly the tool call and tool result at the start of the history, and the goal, the source, and the fact are all there. Later requests cannot see them, so the model can only say it lacks grounds or, worse, make something up.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: A bigger context window does not solve the root problem either. In a long task the history only grows: every file read and every command run adds a tool result, and after dozens of rounds it still won't fit. Even if it fits, every request resends the whole history, usage is billed in tokens, and the longer it is, the more expensive and slower it gets. There is a less obvious layer too: the longer the history, the easier it is for the model to overlook an early fact, and fitting in the window does not mean being used.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: Compression happens between two requests, and the harness does it: it takes the current message history, rewrites part of it, then sends the next request. The model does not decide whether to compress; it only sees the rewritten result. The rewriting can be done entirely by the program, or the model can be asked to write a summary. This lesson compares both kinds of approach.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: This lesson compares three compression methods on the same history. The runner performs two real reads in turn, of messages-context and then application-state, with 8 rounds of side discussion between them. The goal, the first read, and the side discussions count as the earlier part; the second read and the last round of side discussion count as the recent part. All three methods rewrite only the earlier part and keep the recent part as is; one more arm uses no compression, as a control.

section-2.title.text: Probe question: only old information can answer it

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: After compression, you cannot tell from length whether information was lost; you have to ask a question that only old information can answer. A made-up example: compressing a history from 2000 characters to 600 might have only removed repeated side discussions, or it might have removed the key fact along with them. In both cases the character count looks exactly the same.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson's probe question is "最早读取的那份资料来自哪一项？它的原话是什么？" ("Which source did the earliest material come from, and what is its original wording?"). It can be answered only from the result of the first lookup_lesson. The source is messages-context, and the original wording is "模型只看到本次请求里的消息；历史由应用程序重发。" ("The model sees only the messages in this request; the application resends the history."). The report checks for the phrase "历史由应用程序重发" ("the application resends the history"). Both appear only in the earlier part, not in the recent part. Ask once after each arm's compression: if it can be answered, the information survived compression; if not, compression lost it.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: This is the same idea as testing reading comprehension with questions: to know whether someone has read chapter one, ask something only chapter one answers, not something every chapter covers. The uncompressed control arm is asked too, to confirm the probe can be answered at all. If even the control arm cannot answer, the problem is the probe or the model, not the compression.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: The lab report keeps two things apart. Whether the original wording is still in the context is a local string check the program runs on the actual request, and its result is deterministic. Whether the answer gives both the source name and the original wording is a keyword screening; even a hit must be checked against the original text. The first shows whether the information reached the model, and the second shows whether the model used it. A probe checks only one piece of information: it being answered does not mean everything else is still there.

deep-dive-why-compress.title.text: Compression is not only about fitting

deep-dive-why-compress.summary.text: Replacing raw records scattered through the history with organized conclusions makes them easier for the model to use.

deep-dive-why-compress.paragraphs.0.text: The most direct reason for compression is length and cost, but there is another: organized conclusions are easier to use than raw records. A model is very good at finding a ready-made sentence in its context, such as "who placed order 37". Asking it to count and aggregate information scattered across dozens of tool results is error-prone, and it has to count again every time it needs the answer.

deep-dive-why-compress.paragraphs.1.text: A made-up example: an agent checks the status of 30 orders, one tool result each, and 27 are shipped and 3 are refunded. The user asks "how many were refunded", and the model has to count through the 30 results one by one. If the history already contains a line like "Tally so far: shipped 27, refunded 3, order numbers A, B, C", it can simply quote it. Compression writes down, ahead of time, a conclusion that would otherwise take reasoning to reach, as a fact that can be quoted directly.

deep-dive-why-compress.paragraphs.2.text: *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* (深入理解 AI Agent) lists this as the second motive for compression and mentions a third: when a model senses the window is almost used up, it may wrap up before the task is done, and the book argues that compressing early may ease this. So some systems compress once while the window is still far from full. The cost is that the compression itself can go wrong: counts missed, details misremembered, and later requests can only trust it because the raw records are gone. That is also why this lesson checks the compression result with a probe question: what compression writes has to be verified like any other model answer.

deep-dive-why-compress.paragraphs.3.text: There is a cost layer too. The history is resent every round, so the same old content is billed repeatedly. {{lesson:prompt-caching}} covers how providers reuse an identical prefix to cut that cost. Compression rewrites the old history right after the system prompt, so everything from the rewrite onward differs from the previous request and that stretch cannot be reused. The two have to be weighed together.

predict-requests.prompt.text: Before you run "Three compression methods, one probe question" on the lab bench, guess: how many request events will this run produce? Hint: the uncompressed control arm is also asked once, and summary compression sends one extra request first.

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.prompt.text: Why does the probe question ask about the earliest tool result rather than the most recent one?

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.a.text.text: The most recent one is kept as is in every arm, so asking about it would not show any difference among the three methods

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.a.feedback.text: Correct. A probe should ask about the information that compression rewrites.

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.b.text.text: The most recent tool result was made up by the runner

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Both tool results come from real lookup_lesson reads.

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.c.text.text: The model only answers questions about the first message

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The model can see all the messages in the request; the earliest one is asked about because it is the one that compression rewrites.

mq-probe-target.why-earliest.explanation.text: A probe question should depend only on the information being compressed, so that its answer shows what compression lost.

section-3.title.text: Rule-based compression: the program decides what to keep

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Rule-based compression has the program assemble one record from predefined fields, without calling the model, so what is kept and how it is written can be known in advance. The first question is: what in the history will definitely be needed later? For a "look something up, then answer" task like this lesson's, the answer is a fixed set: the goal, the constraints, which sources were read, what facts were found, and what remains to do. Assemble them into one record and it can replace the whole earlier part.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: It is like the form you fill in at a shift handover: not a running log, just fields for the task, cautions, verified facts, and to-dos. The record rule_record builds has five fields: goal, constraints, source, fact, and to-do. The fact field is not rewritten at all; checked_fact takes it directly from the real tool result, so the original wording in the record matches that read character for character. The source field says "第 1 次读取 messages-context" ("read 1: messages-context"), not just a name: the probe asks about the "earliest", so the record has to keep the order.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: After assembly it measures the length first: if the record exceeds char_budget it raises a ValueError, this arm sends no request, and the runner records the reason in lesson.compaction. It would rather not send than quietly delete the source or cut a fact in half: a truncated fact can change its meaning entirely, yet the model will accept it as given. A real system must decide what to do after a refusal, such as switching to another kind of compression or handing off to a person; this lesson demonstrates only the refusal itself.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: The cost of rule-based compression is that the fields are hard-coded. If a side discussion contains a sentence that later turns out to be useful, it belongs to no column and is dropped with the rest. So it suits information whose structure is clear in advance, such as the goal, progress, and verified numbers; the more open-ended the task, the harder it is to list all the fields up front.

section-4.title.text: Clearing old tool results: the position stays, the content is gone

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: Clearing old tool results replaces only the content of the earlier tool message with a one-line note, and the message itself stays where it was. In real long tasks, tool results usually take up most of the space: a file read is thousands of characters and a test run's log can be tens of thousands. Once the model has read these results and made its decisions from them, it mostly doesn't need to read them word for word again, yet they are resent with the history every round.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: clear_old_tool_results first finds the position of every tool message and keeps the latest keep_latest (default 1). The content of earlier ones is replaced with CLEARED: cleared is true, plus a line saying the original content is not in the context. The assistant call and the tool_call_id are untouched, the message count does not change, the call and the tool result are still paired, and the protocol check from {{lesson:messages-context}} still passes. It does not call the model and needs no field design, so it is the least work of the three methods.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: Keeping the position is useful: the model can still see that it once called lookup_lesson with messages-context, only not what the result was. Real systems usually let it call the tool again to look it up, so clearing suits results that can be fetched again, such as file contents and query results. The requests in this lesson deliberately offer no tools, so the model cannot look it up again: the source the probe asks about can still be recognized from the call arguments, but the original wording cannot be answered.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: Two more things to note. For calls that change something outside, such as writing a file or sending a message, the model can still tell from the call record after clearing that the action happened, so it won't assume it never did and repeat it; but if the result will be needed later, it should not be cleared. Also, the tool results in this lesson are short, so clearing saves few characters; the longer the tool result, the more it saves.

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.prompt.text: The probe cannot be answered in the arm that clears old tool results. What is the most likely reason?

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.a.text.text: The content of the earliest tool result was replaced with a note, so the original wording is no longer in the context

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.a.feedback.text: Correct. Clearing leaves only the position; the content is gone, so the model has nothing to answer from.

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.b.text.text: The call and the tool result were split, and the provider rejected the request

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Clearing only swaps the content, the pairing is intact, and the request is valid.

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.c.text.text: The request is too long, and the model can't read the later content

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.c.feedback.text: Not quite. After clearing, the request is actually shorter; the problem is that the information itself is gone.

mq-clear.probe-after-clearing.explanatio.text: A shorter length does not mean the needed information is still there; check with a question that depends only on the old information.

section-5.title.text: Summary compression: the model decides what to keep

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Summary compression sends one extra request that has the model write the earlier part as a summary, and later requests use the summary in place of the earlier part. Its biggest difference from the other two is that the model decides what to keep: rule-based compression knows only fields, clearing knows only positions, but a summary can understand the content and write in even a useful sentence from a side discussion. That is its strength.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: summary_body builds this extra request: the first message is SUMMARY_SYSTEM, which says to write only a summary and not carry on with the task; in the middle is the original text of the earlier part; the last user message is the compression instruction. The runner prefixes the model's answer with "此前对话的摘要：" ("Summary of the earlier conversation:") and puts it into the round-5 request. This extra request also counts toward the model call count; it has to carry the whole earlier part, and its usage is listed separately in the lab report.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: The instruction can influence what the summary keeps. The default instruction asks to keep the goal, the constraints, the source and original result text of every tool call, and unfinished items; the brief instruction, "请用一两句话概括以上对话。" ("Summarize the conversation above in one or two sentences."), asks only for one or two sentences. The original summary text is in the round-4 response; reading it tells you why this arm's probe can or cannot be answered.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: A summary is lossy by nature: it usually keeps the gist and loses original wording, specific numbers, and order. The model writing the summary can also get it wrong, for example by swapping the sources of two pieces of material; the original is gone, so later requests can only trust it. So after summary compression, read the original summary text first, then look at the probe: from the probe answer alone you cannot tell whether the summary lost the information or the model failed to use it.

deep-dive-summary-prompt.title.text: How to write the summary instruction

deep-dive-summary-prompt.summary.text: Let the summary know what comes next and which details must not be lost, and don't let it carry out instructions found in the history.

deep-dive-summary-prompt.paragraphs.0.text: The same history with different instructions gives very different summaries. "Summarize the conversation above" only tells the model to be short, not what comes next, so it naturally writes what it thinks is important. This lesson's default instruction names what to keep: the goal, the constraints, the sources and result text, and the to-dos, and it also gives a length limit.

deep-dive-summary-prompt.paragraphs.1.text: One step further, you can write the upcoming task into the instruction, such as "I'll be answering a certain question next, so keep the information relevant to it." The same material needs different things kept under the two tasks "list the names" and "understand someone's career". The cost is that the summary is tied to the task, and when the task changes, the old summary may no longer be enough.

deep-dive-summary-prompt.paragraphs.2.text: Details are the easiest to lose. A made-up example: the original says "Order 3 refunded 86 yuan on September 12", and it gets compressed to "there was one refund", so the date, the amount, and the order number are all gone, and checking later means looking it up again. The instruction can ask that numbers, dates, file paths, and original wording be copied exactly, and that each fact be annotated with its source so you can go back and look it up when needed.

deep-dive-summary-prompt.paragraphs.3.text: One more point that is easy to overlook: tool results in the earlier part may contain text that looks like instructions, and the model writing the summary should not carry it out. This lesson's SUMMARY_SYSTEM says not to continue the task, precisely so that this request only writes a summary. Some systems also store the user's current request separately and put it back unchanged after compression, instead of letting the summary paraphrase it.

mq-summary.summary-miss.prompt.text: The probe's keyword screening missed in the summary compression arm. What should you look at first?

mq-summary.summary-miss.a.text.text: The original summary text in the round-4 response: whether the source name and original wording made it in

mq-summary.summary-miss.a.feedback.text: Correct. If the summary did not include it, later requests do not have that information.

mq-summary.summary-miss.b.text.text: The message count of the summary compression arm

mq-summary.summary-miss.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The count cannot tell you what the summary says.

mq-summary.summary-miss.c.text.text: Rerun several times until the screening hits

mq-summary.summary-miss.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Rerunning only gets a different sample, and it hides the fact that the summary lost information.

mq-summary.summary-miss.explanation.text: To tell whether summary compression lost information, read the original summary first; the probe result is the second step.

section-7.title.text: When to compress, and how much

section-7.paragraphs.0.text: Real systems usually compress only when the length nears the budget; this lesson compresses unconditionally in every arm, only for comparison. Compress too early and the original, which still fit, is swapped for a lossy version; compress too late and the provider has already rejected the request and the task stops halfway. A common approach is to leave a margin: trigger when a threshold is exceeded, and compress down to well below the threshold in one go so the next round doesn't need to compress again. Learn Claude Code compresses to eighty percent of the threshold.

section-7.paragraphs.1.text: As for which part to compress, this lesson splits it into the earlier part and the recent part, and the recent part is kept as is. That split makes sense: the last few rounds are what the model is working on, and rewriting them is the most likely to interrupt the current step, while the earlier part has mostly been used already. Real systems often do the same, keeping the last few rounds of conversation or the last few tool results and rewriting only what is older.

section-7.paragraphs.2.text: No matter how much gets compressed, a few things have to be preserved separately: the user's current request, the constraints that still apply, and unfinished work. If they are compressed away, the agent may go on with a different goal. This lesson's rule-based compression writes the goal, constraints, and to-dos as fixed fields, and the default summary instruction names them to keep, for that reason.

deep-dive-layered.title.text: How real systems chain several methods together

deep-dive-layered.summary.text: Do the cheap steps that keep the original recoverable first, and the lossy summary that costs an extra request last.

deep-dive-layered.paragraphs.0.text: Real agents seldom use just one kind of compression. A common idea is to order them by cost: first the steps that do not call the model and whose originals can be recovered, and last the summary, which costs an extra request and is lossy.

deep-dive-layered.paragraphs.1.text: Learn Claude Code does it in four steps. Step one: when a single tool result is too large, the full content is saved to a file on disk, and the context keeps only the file path and a preview of the opening. Step two: when there are too many messages, a copy of the full history is saved separately and the middle stretch is replaced with an "archived" marker, with the cut kept away from the gap between a call and its tool result. Step three: if the length still exceeds the threshold, earlier tool results are cleared, keeping only the last few, and the cleared content is likewise saved to disk first. Step four: if it is still over, the model is asked to write a summary. The first three steps can all recover the original by path; only the fourth really loses information.

deep-dive-layered.paragraphs.2.text: Claude Code also does the cheap things first. The official documentation says that when the context is nearly full, it first clears earlier tool results and, if necessary, then summarizes the conversation; your requests and key code snippets are preserved, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost, so rules that must hold for the long term belong in the project's `CLAUDE.md`. After compression, it rereads the project root's `CLAUDE.md` from disk rather than leaving it to the summary to paraphrase. When you run `/compact` by hand, you can add a request, such as `/compact focus on the API changes`, telling the summary what to keep, which works like this lesson's compression instruction. If a tool result is so large that the context is full again right after each summary, it tries a few times, then stops and reports an error rather than looping forever. For details, go by the official documentation.

deep-dive-layered.paragraphs.3.text: Two more details. The trigger is usually that the length exceeds a threshold, not compressing every round. Each compression changes the history's content, and later requests have to reprocess the rewritten part, so it is better to wait until it is nearly full and compress enough in one go. A provider may still reject a request for being too long; you can then compress once and retry, but limit the number of times so you don't get stuck in a loop of compressing and failing again and again.

deep-dive-layered.paragraphs.4.text: This lesson separates the three methods and runs each in full to show what each loses. Real systems chain them and use thresholds to decide how far along the chain to go.

misconception-shorter.claim.text: The request got much shorter after compression and the model's answer reads smoothly, so the information we need must all still be there.

misconception-shorter.correction.text: Length only tells you how much was deleted, and smooth wording only shows the model can write sentences. Whether the information is still there has to be checked with a probe question that depends only on the old information: first see whether the request contains the original wording, then read the answer. The answer from the arm that cleared old tool results can also read smoothly while the original wording is no longer in the request.

section-6.title.text: How to read the lab report

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: In the lab report, look first at the "原话还在上下文里" ("original wording still in the context") column, then the screening, and finally read the original answer text. The table has one row per arm: message count, JSON characters, whether the original wording is still in the context, the probe answer, the screening result, and provider usage. When rule-based compression is refused, its row does not appear; the reason is in the check "规则压缩装下了关键证据" ("rule-based compression fit the key evidence") and in the lesson.compaction event.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: The character count is local JSON length, not tokens; for token counts, look at the provider usage column, which says "未报告" ("not reported") when there is none. When comparing lengths across arms, remember that the summary compression arm also has an extra request: its own request is short, but to get the summary, round 4 already sent the whole earlier part once.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: None of these requests carries tool definitions, but the model still occasionally proposes a tool call instead of writing text; in that case the answer cell says what call it proposed, and the runner does not execute it. One run shows only that run: a screening hit does not mean the answer is correct, and a miss still needs the original text read; a summary is rewritten by the model each time, so another run may keep different things.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: Compression only works within a single run; when the run ends, this message history is no longer used. Some information needs to survive across runs, such as a learning goal the user stated. {{lesson:persistent-memory}} writes that kind of information to a database outside the context and fetches it back on the next run.

mq-not-in-context.phrase-missing-but-ans.text: In one arm, "原话还在上下文里" ("original wording still in the context") is false, yet the answer gives a convincing-looking quote. How should you judge it?
That sentence has no basis in the request; compare it word for word with the tool result from the first read
Correct. The original wording is not in the request, so the sentence the model wrote is either a guess or happens to be close; either way, check it against the tool result.
The local string check missed the original wording
Not quite. The string check looks at the request that was actually sent, and its result is deterministic; the request really does not contain that original wording.
The answer has the original wording, so compression did not lose the information
Not quite. Whether the information was lost is decided by whether the request has it; a sentence appearing in the answer cannot prove, in reverse, that the request had it.
First see whether the information reached the model, then look at the answer; reverse the order and you will treat a made-up answer as evidence.

code-decision.title.text: Three compression methods side by side, compared with the same probe question

code-decision.chosen.text: The same history, with only the earlier part rewritten and the recent part kept as is; rule-based compression refuses if the key evidence does not fit; every arm runs the protocol check before sending; the probe result keeps the local string check and the keyword screening separate.

code-decision.summary-only.why_not.text: The model decides what the summary keeps, so without a probe you cannot know what was lost; each compression also costs an extra request.

code-decision.model-judge.title.text: Ask the model again to judge whether the probe answer is right

code-decision.model-judge.why_not.text: That is yet another request, and the judgment itself can be wrong. This lesson uses keyword screening first and reminds you to check against the original text.

code-decision.delete-tool.title.text: Delete the old tool message outright

code-decision.delete-tool.why_not.text: Deleting the tool result while leaving the assistant call makes the protocol invalid; to delete it, delete it together with the call, and that is the truncation window from {{lesson:context-budget}}.

three-ways.title.text: Three compression methods, one probe question

three-ways.hypothesis.text: Rule-based compression writes the source and fact of the earliest tool result into the record, so the original wording is still in the context; after clearing old tool results, the context no longer has that original wording; after summary compression, whether the original wording is still there depends on the summary the model wrote.

three-ways.compare.label.text: Two reads, 8 rounds of side discussion: no compression, rule-based, clearing old results, summary

three-ways.lookups.text.text: What the two lookup_lesson calls actually returned: messages-context first, then application-state.

three-ways.control.text.text: The uncompressed arm: message count, character count, and the original wording in the context.

three-ways.rule-record.text.text: The rule-based compression record: goal, constraints, source, fact, and to-do in one message.

three-ways.cleared-result.text.text: The first tool result in the clearing arm: the content became a note, and the call and tool result are still paired.

three-ways.cleared-answer.text.text: The original answer text of the clearing arm to the probe question.

three-ways.summary-text.text.text: The original summary the model wrote: are the earliest material's source and original wording still in it?

three-ways.probe-table.text.text: The lab report: for each arm, the length, whether the original wording is still in the context, the probe answer, and the screening result.

three-ways.guide.0.text.text: The four arms' requests ask the same probe question. First see where the two pieces of material come from.

three-ways.guide.1.text.text: Both reads are real local Python executions. The probe asks about the first one.

three-ways.guide.2.text.text: The control arm carries the whole history. Note its character count; the other three arms are compared against it.

three-ways.guide.3.text.text: Rule-based compression replaces the earlier part with this one record, and the source and fact come from the first read.

three-ways.guide.4.text.text: This clearing step does not call the model: it only replaces the first read's tool result with a one-line note.

three-ways.guide.5.text.text: Read the clearing arm's answer: did the model say it lacks grounds, or did it make up an answer?

three-ways.guide.6.text.text: This is the summary the model wrote itself. Look for messages-context and the original wording in it.

three-ways.guide.7.text.text: Finally, compare against the lab report: first see whether the original wording is in the context, then the keyword screening. The screening looks only at keywords, so both hits and misses need checking against the original text.

three-ways.conclusion.proves.0.text: Whether the original wording of the earliest tool result is still in the context that each of the four arms actually sent (a local string check).

three-ways.conclusion.proves.1.text: The summary was written by the current model in this run, and its original text is in the round-4 response; whether the summary compression arm can answer depends directly on what the summary kept.

three-ways.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: The probe screening looks only at keywords; a hit does not mean the answer is correct, and a miss still needs the original text read.

three-ways.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: A probe checks only one piece of information; the summary may have kept this one and lost others.

three-ways.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: Real systems usually let the model call the tool again after old results are cleared, while this experiment's requests offer no tools.

three-ways.conclusion.does_not_prove.3.text: In offline test mode, the summaries and answers are generated by the fixture, not written by a model.

tight-budget.title.text: Rule-based compression's budget cannot hold the evidence

tight-budget.hypothesis.text: When the character budget is smaller than the length the record needs, rule-based compression refuses outright and that arm sends no request; the other arms run as usual, with one fewer model call.

tight-budget.budget-setting.text.text: This run's input: the character budget of the rule-based compression record.

tight-budget.refusal.text.text: The event for when rule-based compression is refused: it states the budget and the characters needed to keep the key evidence.

tight-budget.budget-check.text.text: The lab report's check "规则压缩装下了关键证据" ("rule-based compression fit the key evidence").

tight-budget.call-count.text.text: The model call count in the lab report.

tight-budget.guide.0.text.text: The two arms differ in one input only: the character budget of the rule-based compression record.

tight-budget.guide.1.text.text: This is the char_budget of your run.

tight-budget.guide.2.text.text: When the budget cannot hold it, rule-based compression neither deletes the source nor the fact; it refuses outright, with the reason written here. The arm with enough budget has no such event.

tight-budget.guide.3.text.text: This item in the lab report is truthfully marked as failed, and the results of other arms do not hide it.

tight-budget.guide.4.text.text: The refused arm sent no request; compare the model call counts of the two arms.

tight-budget.conclusion.proves.0.text: When the budget cannot hold the key evidence, rule-based compression refuses and states the reason, and that arm sent no request.

tight-budget.conclusion.proves.1.text: The other arms run as usual, and the model call count is computed from the requests actually sent.

tight-budget.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: A character budget is not a token count; how many tokens fit depends on the provider's tokenization and usage.

tight-budget.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: The refusal only avoids sending an incomplete record; a real system still has to decide what to do next, such as switching to another kind of compression or asking a person.

summary-instruction.title.text: The summary instruction decides what is kept

summary-instruction.hypothesis.text: With the default instruction, which asks to keep the source and original result text, the summary is more likely to keep the earliest material; with one that asks for only one or two sentences, the summary is more likely to lose the source name and original wording, and the summary compression arm's probe then cannot be answered.

summary-instruction.compare.label.text: Default instruction: keep the source and original result text

summary-instruction.brief-summary.label.text: Brief instruction: summarize in one or two sentences

summary-instruction.instruction.text.text: The summary instruction used this time: it is the last user message of the summary request, and the runner recorded a separate copy before sending.

summary-instruction.summary.text.text: The original summary the model wrote.

summary-instruction.phrase-kept.text.text: Whether the summary compression arm's context still has the original wording (a local string check).

summary-instruction.summary-answer.text.text: The original answer text of the summary compression arm to the probe question.

summary-instruction.guide.0.text.text: The two arms differ only in the summary instruction. First see which one was used this time.

summary-instruction.guide.1.text.text: This is this run's summary instruction. It is the last user message of the summary request, and before it is the original text of the earlier part.

summary-instruction.guide.2.text.text: Read the original summary: were messages-context and the original wording written in?

summary-instruction.guide.3.text.text: The program checks whether the original wording is still there before sending. This result depends only on what the summary wrote.

summary-instruction.guide.4.text.text: Finally, read this arm's probe answer and compare it with the other arm.

summary-instruction.conclusion.proves.0.text: The summary instructions of the two runs, the original summaries the model wrote, and whether the original wording is still in the summary compression arm's context.

summary-instruction.conclusion.does_not_.text: One comparison cannot show which instruction is always better; with the same instruction, another sample may produce a different summary.
That the summary kept the original wording does not guarantee it kept the other information needed later.
In offline test mode, the summaries are generated by the fixture, not written by a model.

inputs.char_budget.help.text: The maximum JSON characters the rule-based compression record allows; if the key evidence does not fit, that arm is refused.

inputs.summary_style.options.keep_source.text: Keep the source and original result text

inputs.summary_style.options.brief.label.text: Summarize in one or two sentences

quiz.rule-overflow.prompt.text: The rule-based compression record exceeds the character budget. What is the right thing to do?

quiz.rule-overflow.a.text.text: Raise an error stating the budget and the characters needed, and send no request for that arm

quiz.rule-overflow.a.feedback.text: Correct. Better not to send than to send a record that lacks the evidence.

quiz.rule-overflow.b.text.text: Delete the source and keep only the fact

quiz.rule-overflow.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A fact without a source can't be checked, and the model can't say where the grounds are.

quiz.rule-overflow.c.text.text: Cut off the second half of the fact to squeeze it into the budget

quiz.rule-overflow.c.feedback.text: Not quite. A truncated original wording can change its meaning entirely, and then the probe can't be answered correctly.

quiz.rule-overflow.explanation.text: Rule-based compression promises that key evidence is either kept whole or an explicit error is raised.

quiz.clear-count.prompt.text: After old tool results are cleared, what happens to the message count in the request?

quiz.clear-count.a.text.text: It does not change; only the content of the earlier tool result became a note

quiz.clear-count.a.feedback.text: Correct. The position and the pairing are kept, and the content is replaced.

quiz.clear-count.b.text.text: Two fewer, as the call and the tool result are deleted together

quiz.clear-count.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Deleting them together is the truncation window's approach; clearing only swaps the content.

quiz.clear-count.c.text.text: One more, to hold the clearing note

quiz.clear-count.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The note is written into the content of the original tool message, with no extra message.

quiz.clear-count.explanation.text: Clearing keeps the protocol and the position, and the cost is the content.

quiz.screen-hit.prompt.text: The probe's keyword screening hit in the summary compression arm. What can you conclude?

quiz.screen-hit.a.text.text: The answer contains both the source name and the original wording, and the original text still has to be read to confirm it is right

quiz.screen-hit.a.feedback.text: Correct. The screening looks only at keywords, so the conclusion has to be checked against the original text.

quiz.screen-hit.b.text.text: The summary kept all the information in the earlier part

quiz.screen-hit.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A probe checks only one piece of information, and other information may already be lost.

quiz.screen-hit.c.text.text: Summary compression is always better than rule-based compression

quiz.screen-hit.c.feedback.text: Not quite. One run cannot show typical behavior, and the two methods lose different things.

quiz.screen-hit.explanation.text: A screening result is only a starting point: it shows that the keywords appeared, not that the answer is right, nor that other information is still there.

quiz.visible-but-missed.prompt.text: In the lab report, one arm has "原话还在上下文里" ("original wording still in the context") as true, but the probe screening missed. What is the most likely situation?

quiz.visible-but-missed.a.text.text: The information reached the model, but the answer did not give both the source name and the original wording

quiz.visible-but-missed.a.feedback.text: Correct. Read the original answer: it may have reworded the original, or it may not have used the information.

quiz.visible-but-missed.b.text.text: The local string check is wrong

quiz.visible-but-missed.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The string check only looks at whether the original wording appears verbatim in the request, and its result is deterministic.

quiz.visible-but-missed.c.text.text: The provider did not receive that message

quiz.visible-but-missed.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The request event records what was actually sent, and the original wording is in it.

quiz.visible-but-missed.explanation.text: Writing the two checks separately is what lets you tell whether the information didn't arrive or the model didn't use it.

quiz.summary-extra-cost.prompt.text: Compared with rule-based compression, what extra does summary compression cost?

quiz.summary-extra-cost.a.text.text: One more model request, and that request has to carry the whole original text of the earlier part

quiz.summary-extra-cost.a.feedback.text: Correct. The round-4 summary request counts toward the model call count, and its usage is listed separately in the lab report.

quiz.summary-extra-cost.b.text.text: Nothing extra; both the summary and the rule record are generated by the program

quiz.summary-extra-cost.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The rule record is assembled by the program, but the summary is written by the model and needs an extra request.

quiz.summary-extra-cost.c.text.text: An extra tool definition, so the model can reread the material

quiz.summary-extra-cost.c.feedback.text: Not quite. None of this lesson's requests carries tool definitions, so the model can't reread anything.

quiz.summary-extra-cost.explanation.text: A summary can understand the content; the cost is one more request, and the summary itself may lose information or be wrong.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Find the tool result that was replaced with a note in the request of the arm that clears old tool results.

check-hunt.explanation.text: This is the fourth message of the round-3 request: the tool_call_id is unchanged and the assistant call before it is still there; only the content became a note with cleared set to true. The message count equals that of the uncompressed arm, and the original wording is no longer in this request.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source code, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I compared the message counts and character counts of the four arms' requests, and I can say which part each compression method rewrites.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I can tell that "原话还在上下文里" ("original wording still in the context") and a probe screening hit are two different checks.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I read the original summary in round 4 and can say why the summary compression arm's probe can or cannot be answered.

check-points.item-4.text.text: Small extension: change the default of keep_latest in clear_old_tool_results to 0 (clear both tool results), restart the backend and run again, and see which piece of material is left in the clearing arm's context.

code_notes.char_budget.note.text: This lesson's input: the maximum JSON characters the rule-based compression record allows; if the key evidence does not fit, that arm is refused.

code_notes.lookup_lesson.note.text: A local tool: returns the source and fact of a piece of reference material by source_key, really executed each time.

code_notes.lesson.compaction.note.text: This lesson's event: records the character count and whether the original wording is still in the context for each arm; records the reason when rule-based compression is refused; records the instruction before the summary request.

code_notes.keep_latest.note.text: How many of the latest tool results to keep when clearing, default 1; the content of earlier tool results is replaced with a note.
